entries.6270ee7d9698acb662b9a366f149cbe4cf6c8cb4: <div sID="gen7962" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="1Chr.29" sID="1Chr.29"/> <div eID="gen7962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7963" type="x-p"/> David has said what he had to say to Solomon. But he had something more to say to the congregation before he parted with them. I. He pressed them to contribute, according to their ability, towards the building and furnishing of the temple, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1-1Chr.29.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. They made their presents accordingly with great generosity, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6-1Chr.29.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. III. David offered up solemn prayers and praises to God upon that occasion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10-1Chr.29.20">ver. 10-20</reference>), with sacrifices, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.21-1Chr.29.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. IV. Solomon was hereupon enthroned, with great joy and magnificence, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23-1Chr.29.25">ver. 23-25</reference>. V. David, soon after this finished his course, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.30">ver. 26-30</reference>. And it is hard to say which shines brighter here, the setting sun or the rising sun.
entries.3df1db73f68a5f6bced9aae1df2db59ff6417eff: <div eID="gen7963" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Presents for the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen7964" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Furthermore David the king said unto all the congregation, Solomon my son, whom alone God hath chosen, <hi type="italic">is yet</hi> young and tender, and the work <hi type="italic">is</hi> great: for the palace <hi type="italic">is</hi> not for man, but for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now I have prepared with all my might for the house of my God the gold for <hi type="italic">things to be made</hi> of gold, and the silver for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of silver, and the brass for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of brass, the iron for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of iron, and wood for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of wood; onyx stones, and <hi type="italic">stones</hi> to be set, glistering stones, and of divers colours, and all manner of precious stones, and marble stones in abundance. <hi type="super">3</hi> Moreover, because I have set my affection to the house of my God, I have of mine own proper good, of gold and silver, <hi type="italic">which</hi> I have given to the house of my God, over and above all that I have prepared for the holy house, <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">Even</hi> three thousand talents of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and seven thousand talents of refined silver, to overlay the walls of the houses <hi type="italic">withal:</hi> <hi type="super">5</hi> The gold for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of gold, and the silver for <hi type="italic">things</hi> of silver, and for all manner of work <hi type="italic">to be made</hi> by the hands of artificers. And who <hi type="italic">then</hi> is willing to consecrate his service this day unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="super">6</hi> Then the chief of the fathers and princes of the tribes of Israel, and the captains of thousands and of hundreds, with the rulers of the king's work, offered willingly, <hi type="super">7</hi> And gave for the service of the house of God of gold five thousand talents and ten thousand drams, and of silver ten thousand talents, and of brass eighteen thousand talents, and one hundred thousand talents of iron. <hi type="super">8</hi> And they with whom <hi type="italic">precious</hi> stones were found gave <hi type="italic">them</hi> to the treasure of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , by the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then the people rejoiced, for that they offered willingly, because with perfect heart they offered willingly to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and David the king also rejoiced with great joy. <div eID="gen7964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7965" type="x-p"/> We may here observe, <div eID="gen7965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> I. How handsomely David spoke to the great men of Israel, to engage them to contribute towards the building of the temple. It is our duty to <hi type="italic">provoke one another to love and to good works,</hi> not only to do good ourselves, but to draw in others to do good too as much as we can. There were many very rich men in Israel; they were all to share in the benefit of the temple, and of those peaceable days which were to befriend the building of it; and therefore, though David would not impose on them, as a tax, what they should give towards it, he would recommend the present as a fair occasion for a free-will offering, because what is done in works of piety and charity should be done willingly and not by constraint; for God loves a cheerful giver. 1. He would have them consider that Solomon was young and tender, and needed help; but that he was the person whom God had chosen to do this work, and therefore was well worthy their assistance. It is good service to encourage those in the work of God that are as yet young and tender. 2. That the world was great, and all hands should contribute to the carrying of it on. The palace to be built was not for man, but for the Lord God; and the more was contributed towards the building the more magnificent it would be, and therefore the better would it answer the intention. 3. He tells them what great preparations had been made for this work. He did not intend to throw all the burden upon them, nor that it should be built wholly by contributions, but that they should show their good will, by adding to what was done (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have prepared with all my might,</hi> that is, "I have made it my business." Work for God must be done with all our might, or we shall bring nothing to pass in it. 4. He sets them a good example. Besides what was dedicated to this service out of the spoils and presents of the neighbouring nations, which was for the building of the house (of which before, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.14">ch. xxii. 14</reference>), he had, out of his own share, offered largely for the beautifying and enriching of it, 3000 talents of gold and 7000 talents of silver (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.4-1Chr.29.5">v. 4, 5</reference>), and this because he had set his affection on the house of his God. He gave all this, not as Papists build churches, in commutation of penance, or to make atonement for sin, nor as Pharisees give alms, to be seen of men; but purely because he loved the habitation of God's house; so he professed (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.8">Ps. xxvi. 8</reference>) and here he proved it. Those who set their affection upon the service of God will think no pains nor cost too much to bestow upon it; and then our offerings are pleasing to God when they come from love. Those that set their affection on things above will set their affection on the house of God, through which our way to heaven lies. Now this he gives them an account of, to stir them up to do likewise. Note, Those who would draw others to do that which is good must themselves lead. Those especially who are advanced above others in place and dignity should particularly contrive how to make their light shine before men, because the influence of their example is more powerful and extensive than that of other people. 5. He stirs them up to do as he had done (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">And who then is willing to concecrate his service this day unto the Lord?</hi> (1.) We must each of us, in our several places, serve the Lord, and consecrate our service to him, separate it from other things that are foreign and interfere with it, and direct and design it for the honour and glory of God. (2.) We must make the service of God our business, must <hi type="italic">fill our hands to the Lord,</hi> so the Hebrew phrase is. Those who engage themselves in the service of God will have their hands full; there is work enough for the whole man in that service. The filling of our hands with the service of God intimates that we must serve him only, serve him liberally, and serve him in the strength of grace derived from him. (3.) We must be free herein, do it willingly and speedily, do it this day, when we are in a good mind. <hi type="italic">Who is willing?</hi> Now let him show it. <div eID="gen7966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7967" type="x-p"/> II. How handsomely they all contributed towards the building of the temple when they were thus stirred up to it. Though they were persuaded to it, yet it is said, <hi type="italic">They offered willingly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6">v. 6</reference>. So he said who knew their hearts. Nay, they offered <hi type="italic">with a perfect heart,</hi> from a good principle and with a sincere respect to the glory of God, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.9">v. 9</reference>. How generous they were appears by the sum total of the contributions, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.7">v. 7, 8</reference>. They gave like themselves, like princes, like princes of Israel. And a pleasant day's work it was; for, 1. <hi type="italic">The people rejoiced,</hi> which may be meant of the people themselves that offered: they were glad of the opportunity of honouring God thus with their substance, and glad of the prospect of bringing this good work to perfection. Or the common people rejoiced in the generosity of their princes, that they had such rulers over them as were forward to this good work. Every Israelite is glad to see temple work carried on with vigour. 2. <hi type="italic">David rejoiced with great joy</hi> to see the good effects of his psalms and the other helps of devotion he had furnished them with, rejoiced that his son and successor would have those about him that were so well affected to the house of God, and that this work, upon which his heart was so much set, was likely to go on. Note, It is a great reviving to good men, when they are leaving the world, to see those they leave behind zealous for religion and likely to keep it up. <hi type="italic">Lord, now let thou thy servant depart in peace.</hi>
entries.fa48cc2c13ccad15fda62aafeed5c3e376d41434: <div eID="gen7967" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Prayer to God; Sacrifices Offered. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Wherefore David blessed the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> before all the congregation: and David said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> thou, <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel our father, for ever and ever. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thine, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">is</hi> the greatness, and the power, and the glory, and the victory, and the majesty: for all <hi type="italic">that is</hi> in the heaven and in the earth <hi type="italic">is thine;</hi> thine <hi type="italic">is</hi> the kingdom, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thou art exalted as head above all. <hi type="super">12</hi> Both riches and honour <hi type="italic">come</hi> of thee, and thou reignest over all; and in thine hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> power and might; and in thine hand <hi type="italic">it is</hi> to make great, and to give strength unto all. <hi type="super">13</hi> Now therefore, our God, we thank thee, and praise thy glorious name. <hi type="super">14</hi> But who <hi type="italic">am</hi> I, and what <hi type="italic">is</hi> my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly after this sort? for all things <hi type="italic">come</hi> of thee, and of thine own have we given thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> For we <hi type="italic">are</hi> strangers before thee, and sojourners, as <hi type="italic">were</hi> all our fathers: our days on the earth <hi type="italic">are</hi> as a shadow, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> none abiding. <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God, all this store that we have prepared to build thee a house for thine holy name <hi type="italic">cometh</hi> of thine hand, and <hi type="italic">is</hi> all thine own. <hi type="super">17</hi> I know also, my God, that thou triest the heart, and hast pleasure in uprightness. As for me, in the uprightness of mine heart I have willingly offered all these things: and now have I seen with joy thy people, which are present here, to offer willingly unto thee.   18 <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel, our fathers, keep this for ever in the imagination of the thoughts of the heart of thy people, and prepare their heart unto thee: <hi type="super">19</hi> And give unto Solomon my son a perfect heart, to keep thy commandments, thy testimonies, and thy statutes, and to do all <hi type="italic">these things,</hi> and to build the palace, <hi type="italic">for</hi> the which I have made provision. <hi type="super">20</hi> And David said to all the congregation, Now bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. And all the congregation blessed the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers, and bowed down their heads, and worshipped the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the king. <hi type="super">21</hi> And they sacrificed sacrifices unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and offered burnt offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , on the morrow after that day, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a thousand bullocks, a thousand rams, <hi type="italic">and</hi> a thousand lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel: <hi type="super">22</hi> And did eat and drink before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king the second time, and anointed <hi type="italic">him</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">to be</hi> the chief governor, and Zadok <hi type="italic">to be</hi> priest. <div eID="gen7968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen7969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> I. The solemn address which David made to God upon occasion of the noble subscriptions of the princes towards the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore David blessed the Lord,</hi> not only alone in his closet, but <hi type="italic">before all the congregation.</hi> This I expected when we read (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.9">v. 9</reference>) that <hi type="italic">David rejoiced with great joy;</hi> for such a devout man as he would no doubt make that the matter of his thanksgiving which was so much the matter of his rejoicing. He that looked round with comfort would certainly look up with praise. David was now old and looked upon himself as near his end; and it well becomes aged saints, and dying saints, to have their hearts much enlarged in praise and thanksgiving. This will silence their complaints of their bodily infirmities, and help to make the prospect of death itself less gloomy. David's psalms, toward the latter end of the book, are most of them psalms of praise. The nearer we come to the world of everlasting praise the more we should speak the language and do the work of that world. In this address, <div eID="gen7970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> 1. He adores God, and ascribes glory to him as the God of Israel, <hi type="italic">blessed for ever and ever.</hi> Our Lord's prayer ends with a doxology much like this which David here begins with—<hi type="italic">for thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory.</hi> This is properly praising God—with holy awe and reverence, and agreeable affection, acknowledging, (1.) His infinite perfections; not only that he is great, powerful, glorious, &c., but that his is the greatness, power, and glory, that is, he has them in and of himself, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">v. 11</reference>. He is the fountain and centre of every thing that is bright and blessed. All that we can, in our most exalted praises, attribute to him he has an unquestionable title to. His is the <hi type="italic">greatness;</hi> his greatness is immense and incomprehensible; and all others are little, are nothing, in comparison of him. His is the <hi type="italic">power,</hi> and it is almighty and irresistible; power belongs to him, and all the power of all the creatures is derived from him and depends upon him. His is the <hi type="italic">glory;</hi> for his glory is his own end and the end of the whole creation. All the glory we can give him with our hearts, lips, and lives, comes infinitely short of what is his due. His is the <hi type="italic">victory;</hi> he transcends and surpasses all, and is able to conquer and subdue all things to himself; and his victories are incontestable and uncontrollable. And his is the <hi type="italic">majesty,</hi> real and personal; with him is terrible majesty, inexpressible and inconceivable. (2.) His sovereign dominion, as rightful owner and possessor of all: "<hi type="italic">All that is in the heaven, and in the earth, is thine,</hi> and at thy disposal, by the indisputable right of creation, and as supreme ruler and commander of all: <hi type="italic">thine is the kingdom,</hi> and all kings are thy subjects; for thou art head, and art to be exalted and worshipped as head above all." (3.) His universal influence and agency. All that are rich and honourable among the children of men have their riches and honours from God. This acknowledgment he would have the princes take notice of and join in, that they might not think they had merited any thing of God by their generosity; for from God they had their riches and honour, and what they had returned to him was but a small part of what they had received from him. Whoever are great among men, it is God's hand that makes them so; and, whatever strength we have, it is God that gives it to us, as the <hi type="italic">God of Israel our father,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10 Ps.68.35">v. 10. Ps. lxviii. 35</reference>. <div eID="gen7971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> 2. He acknowledges with thankfulness the grace of God enabling them to contribute so cheerfully towards the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.13-1Chr.29.14">v. 13, 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Now therefore, our God, we thank thee.</hi> Note, The more we do for God the more we are indebted to him for the honour of being employed in his service, and for grace enabling us, in any measure, to serve him. <hi type="italic">Does he</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">thank that servant?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.9">Luke xvii. 9</reference>. No: but that servant has a great deal of reason to thank him. He thanks God that they were <hi type="italic">able to offer so willingly.</hi> Note, (1.) It is a great instance of the power of God's grace in us to be able to do the work of God willingly. He works <hi type="italic">both to will and to do;</hi> and it is in the day of his power that his people are made willing, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. (2.) We must give God all the glory of all the good that is at any time done by ourselves or others. Our own good works must not be the matter of our pride, nor the good works of others the matter of our flattery, but both the matter of our praise; for certainly it is the greatest honour and pleasure in the world faithfully to serve God. <div eID="gen7972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7973" type="x-p"/> 3. He speaks very humbly of himself, and his people, and the offerings they had now presented to God. (1.) For himself, and those that joined with him, though they were princes, he wondered that God should take such notice of them and do so much for them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who am I, and what is my people?</hi> David was the most honourable person, and Israel the most honourable person, then in the world; yet thus does he speak of himself and them, as unworthy the divine cognizance and favour. David now looks very great, presiding in an august assembly, appointing his successor, and making a noble present to the honour of God; and yet he is little and low in his own eyes: <hi type="italic">Who am I, O Lord?</hi> for (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.15">v. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">we are strangers before thee, and sojourners,</hi> poor despicable creatures. Angels in heaven are at home there; saints on earth are but strangers here: <hi type="italic">Our days on the earth are as a shadow.</hi> David's days had as much of substance in them as most men's; for he was a great man, a good man, a useful man, and now an old man, one that lived long and lived to good purpose: and yet he puts himself not only into the number, but in the front, of those who must acknowledge that their <hi type="italic">days on the earth are as a shadow,</hi> which intimates that our life is a vain life, a dark life, a transient life, and a life that will have its periods either in perfect light or perfect darkness. The next words explain it: <hi type="italic">There is no abiding,</hi> Heb. <hi type="italic">no expectation.</hi> We cannot expect any great matters from it, nor can we expect any long continuance of it. This is mentioned here as that which forbids us to boast of the service we do to God. Alas! it is confined to a scantling of time, it is the service of a frail and short life, and therefore what can we pretend to merit by it? (2.) As to their offerings, <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">of thy own have we given thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">v. 14</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">It cometh of thy hand, and is all thy own.</hi> "We have it from thee as a free gift, and therefore are bound to use it for thee; and what we present to thee is but rent or interest from thy own." "In like manner" (says bishop Patrick) "we ought to acknowledge God in all spiritual things, referring every good thought, good purpose, good work, to his grace, from whom we receive it." <hi type="italic">Let him that glories</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">glory in the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen7973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7974" type="x-p"/> 4. He appeals to God concerning his own sincerity in what he did, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.17">v. 17</reference>. It is a great satisfaction to a good man to think that God <hi type="italic">tries the heart</hi> and <hi type="italic">has pleasure in uprightness,</hi> that, whoever may misinterpret or contemn it, he is acquainted with and approves of the <hi type="italic">way of the righteous.</hi> It was David's comfort that God knew with what pleasure he both offered his own and saw the people's offering. He was neither proud of his own good work nor envious of the good works of others. <div eID="gen7974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7975" type="x-p"/> 5. He prays to God both for the people and for Solomon, that both might hold on as they began. In this prayer he addresses God as <hi type="italic">the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob,</hi> a God in covenant with them and with us for their sakes. Lord, give us grace to make good our part of the covenant, that we may not forfeit the benefit of it. Or thus: they were kept in their integrity by the grace of God establishing their way; let the same grace that was sufficient for them be so for us. (1.) For the people he prays (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.18">v. 18</reference>) that what good God had put into their minds he would always keep there, that they might never be worse than they were now, might never lose the convictions they were now under, nor cool in their affections to the house of God, but always have the same thoughts of things as they now seemed to have. Great consequences depend upon what is innermost, and what uppermost, in the imagination of the thoughts of our heart, what we aim at and what we love to think of. If any good have got possession of our hearts, or the hearts of our friends, it is good by prayer to commit the custody of it to the grace of God: "Lord, keep it there, keep it for ever there. David has prepared materials for the temple; but, Lord, do thou prepare their hearts for such a privilege;" <hi type="italic">establish</hi> their hearts, so the <hi type="italic">margin.</hi> "Confirm their resolutions. They are in a good mind; keep them so when I am gone, them and theirs for ever." (2.) For Solomon he prays (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.19">v. 19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Give him a perfect heart.</hi> He had charged him (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.9">ch. xxviii. 9</reference>) to serve God <hi type="italic">with a perfect heart;</hi> now here he prays to God to give him such a heart. He does not pray, "Lord, make him a rich man, a great man, a learned man;" but, "Lord, make him an honest man;" for that is better than all. "Lord, <hi type="italic">give him a perfect heart,</hi> not only in general <hi type="italic">to keep thy commandments,</hi> but in particular <hi type="italic">to build the palace,</hi> that he may do that service with a single eye." Yet his building the house would not prove him to have a perfect heart unless he made conscience of keeping God's commandments. It is not helping to build churches that will save us if we live in disobedience to God's law. <div eID="gen7975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7976" type="x-p"/> II. The cheerful concurrence of this great assembly in this great solemnity. 1. They joined with David in the adoration of God. When he had done his prayer he called to them to testify their concurrence (<hi type="italic">Now bless the Lord your God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.20">v. 20</reference>), which accordingly they did, by <hi type="italic">bowing down their heads,</hi> a gesture of adoration. Whoever is the mouth of the congregation, those only have the benefit who join with him, not by <hi type="italic">bowing down the head</hi> so much as by <hi type="italic">lifting up the soul.</hi> 2. They paid their respects to the king, looking upon him as an instrument in God's hand of much good to them; and, in honouring him, they honoured God. 3. The next day they offered abundance of sacrifices to God (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.21">v. 21</reference>), both burnt-offerings, which were wholly consumed, and peace-offerings, which the offerer had the greatest part of to himself. Hereby they testified a generous gratitude to God for the good posture their public affairs were in, though David was going the way of all the earth. 4. They feasted and rejoiced before God, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.22">v. 22</reference>. In token of their joy in God, and communion with him, they feasted upon their peace-offerings in a religious manner before the Lord. What had been offered to God they feasted upon, by which was intimated to them that they should be never the poorer for their late liberal contributions to the service of the temple; they themselves should feast upon the comfort of it. 5. They made Solomon king the second time. He having been before anointed in haste, upon occasion of Adonijah's rebellion, it was thought fit to repeat the ceremony, for the greater satisfaction of the people. They <hi type="italic">anointed him to the Lord.</hi> Magistrates must look upon themselves as set apart for God, to be his ministers, and must rule accordingly in the fear of God. Zadok also was anointed to be priest in the room of Abiathar, who had lately forfeited his honour. Happy art thou, O Israel! under such a prince and such a pontiff.
entries.cec838f4b924da0afedd75db6751642f49d1e038: <div eID="gen7976" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Solomon Magnified. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> Then Solomon sat on the throne of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> as king instead of David his father, and prospered; and all Israel obeyed him. <hi type="super">24</hi> And all the princes, and the mighty men, and all the sons likewise of king David, submitted themselves unto Solomon the king. <hi type="super">25</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed upon him <hi type="italic">such</hi> royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel. <hi type="super">26</hi> Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the time that he reigned over Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> forty years; seven years reigned he in Hebron, and thirty and three <hi type="italic">years</hi> reigned he in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">28</hi> And he died in a good old age, full of days, riches, and honour: and Solomon his son reigned in his stead. <hi type="super">29</hi> Now the acts of David the king, first and last, behold, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer, <hi type="super">30</hi> With all his reign and his might, and the times that went over him, and over Israel, and over all the kingdoms of the countries. <div eID="gen7977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> These verses bring king Solomon to his throne and king David to his grave. Thus the rising generation thrusts out that which went before, and says, "Make room for us." Every one has his day. <div eID="gen7978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> I. Here is Solomon rising (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23">v. 23</reference>): <hi type="italic">Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord.</hi> Not his throne which he prepared in the heavens, but the throne of Israel is called <hi type="italic">the throne of the Lord</hi> because not only is he King of all nations, and all kings rule under him, but he was in a peculiar manner King of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Sam.12.12">1 Sam. xii. 12</reference>. He had the founding, he had the filling, of their throne, by immediate direction. The municipal laws of their kingdom were divine. Urim and prophets were the privy counsellors of their princes; therefore is their throne called <hi type="italic">the throne of the Lord.</hi> Solomon's kingdom typified the kingdom of the Messiah, and his is indeed <hi type="italic">the throne of the Lord;</hi> for the Father judgeth no man, but hath committed all judgment to him; hence he calls him <hi type="italic">his King,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.6">Ps. ii. 6</reference>. Being set on the <hi type="italic">throne of the Lord,</hi> the throne to which God called him, he prospered. Those that follow the divine guidance may expect success by the divine blessing. Solomon prospered; for, 1. His people paid honour to him, as one to whom honour is due: <hi type="italic">All Israel obeyed him,</hi> that is, were ready to swear allegiance to him (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23">v. 23</reference>), the <hi type="italic">princes and mighty men,</hi> and even <hi type="italic">the sons of David,</hi> though by seniority their title to the crown was prior to his, and they might think themselves wronged by his advancement. God thought fit to make him king, and made him fit to be so, and therefore they all <hi type="italic">submitted themselves to him.</hi> God inclined their hearts to do so, that his reign might, from the first, be peaceable. His father was a better man than he, and yet came to the crown with much difficulty, after long delay, and by many and slow steps. David had more faith, and therefore had it more tried. <hi type="italic">They submitted themselves</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">They gave the hand under Solomon</hi>), that is, bound themselves by oath to be true to him (putting the hand under the thigh was a ceremony anciently used in swearing); or they were so entirely devoted that they would put their hand under his feet to serve him. 2. God put honour upon him; for those that honour him he will honour: <hi type="italic">The Lord magnified Solomon exceedingly,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.25">v. 25</reference>. His very countenance and presence, I am apt to think, had something in them very great and awful. All he said and all he did commanded respect. None of all the judges or kings of Israel, his predecessors, made such a figure as he did nor lived in such splendour. <div eID="gen7979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> II. Here is David's setting, that great man going off the stage. The historian here brings him to the end of his day, leaves him asleep, and draws the curtains about him. <div eID="gen7980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> 1. He gives a summary account of the years of his reign, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. He reigned forty years, as did Moses, Othniel, Deborah, Gideon, Eli, Samuel, and Saul, who were before him, and Solomon after him. <div eID="gen7981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives a short account of his death (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.28">v. 28</reference>), that he died <hi type="italic">full of days, riches, and honour;</hi> that is, (1.) Loaded with them. He was very old, and very rich, and very much honoured both of God and man. He had been a man of war from his youth, and, as such, had his soul continually in his hand; yet he was not cut off in the midst of his days, but was preserved through all dangers of a military life, lived to a good old age, and died in peace, died in his bed, and yet in the bed of honour. (2.) Satiated with them. He was <hi type="italic">full of days, riches, and honour;</hi> that is, he had enough of this world and of the riches and honours of it, and knew when he had enough, for he was very willing to die and leave it, having said (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.15">Ps. xlix. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">God shall receive me,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Ps. xxiii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou art with me.</hi> A good man will soon be full of days, riches, and honour, but will never be satisfied with them; no satisfaction but in God's loving kindness. <div eID="gen7982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> 3. For a fuller account of David's life and reign he refers to the histories or records of those times, which were written by Samuel while he lived, and continued, after his death, by Nathan and Gad, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">v. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">There</hi> was related what was observable in his government at home and his wars abroad, <hi type="italic">the times,</hi> that is, the events of <hi type="italic">the times, that went over him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29-1Chr.29.30">v. 29, 30</reference>. These registers were then in being, but are now lost. Note, Good use may be made of those histories of the church which are authentic though not sacred or of divine inspiration.  <chapter eID="1Chr.29"/> <div eID="gen7983" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen7612" osisID="1Chr" type="book"/>

entries.93c0c0f804ad497a43788fe482b194ab8f634115: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3904"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <div sID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1-1Chr.29.9">1Ch 29:1-9</reference>. David Causes the Princes and People to Offer for the House of God.<div eID="gen5617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3904"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Solomon ... is yet young and tender--</hi>Though Solomon was very young when he was raised to the sovereign power, his kingdom escaped the woe pronounced (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ec 10:16</reference>). Mere childhood in a prince is not always a misfortune to a nation, as there are instances of the government being wisely administered during a minority. Solomon himself is a most illustrious proof that a young prince may prove a great blessing; for when he was but a mere child, with respect to his age, no nation was happier. His father, however, made this address before Solomon was endowed with the divine gift of wisdom, and David's reference to his son's extreme youth, in connection with the great national undertaking he had been divinely appointed to execute, was to apologize to this assembly of the estates--or, rather, to assign the reason of his elaborate preparations for the work. <div eID="gen5618" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfbd02ecf7dfc1d1cca89fe2573c6e5a8506138a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3905"/><div sID="gen5619" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3905"/><hi type="bold">3-4. Moreover ... I have of mine own proper good, &c.--</hi>In addition to the immense amount of gold and silver treasure which David had already bequeathed for various uses in the service of the temple, he now made an additional contribution destined to a specific purpose--that of overlaying the walls of the house. This voluntary gift was from the private fortune of the royal donor, and had been selected with the greatest care. The gold was "the gold of Ophir," then esteemed the purest and finest in the world (<reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.13.12">Is 13:12</reference>). The amount was three thousand talents of gold and seven thousand talents of refined silver. <div eID="gen5619" type="x-p"/>
entries.bf6ae985aba0cf609181d996a82783607ba8cc55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3906"/><div sID="gen5620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3906"/><hi type="bold">5. who then is willing to consecrate his service--</hi>Hebrew, "fill his hand"; that is, make an offering (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.29">Ex 32:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.8.33">Le 8:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.33">1Ki 13:33</reference>). The meaning is, that whoever would contribute voluntarily, as he had done, would be offering a freewill offering to the Lord. It was a sacrifice which every one of them could make, and in presenting which the offerer himself would be the priest. David, in asking freewill offerings for the temple, imitated the conduct of Moses in reference to the tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.1-Exod.25.8">Ex 25:1-8</reference>). <div eID="gen5620" type="x-p"/>
entries.e96dacab6b8e3c25156d8af31e63ea7e74ac1cec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3907"/><div sID="gen5621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3907"/><hi type="bold">6-8. Then the chief of the fathers--</hi>or heads of the fathers (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.31">1Ch 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.1">27:1</reference>).<div eID="gen5621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5622" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">princes of the tribes--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.16-1Chr.27.22">1Ch 27:16-22</reference>).<div eID="gen5622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5623" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rulers of the king's work--</hi>those who had charge of the royal demesnes and other possessions (<reference osisRef="1Chr.27.25-1Chr.27.31">1Ch 27:25-31</reference>).<div eID="gen5623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offered willingly--</hi>Influenced by the persuasive address and example of the king, they acted according to their several abilities, and their united contributions amounted to the gross sum--of gold 5,000 talents and 10,000 drams; and of silver, 10,000 talents, besides brass and iron. <div eID="gen5624" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f8d0545621bf944b137544616ab47dad4cd448e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3910"/><div sID="gen5629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3910"/><hi type="bold">10-19. Wherefore David blessed the Lord--</hi>This beautiful thanksgiving prayer was the effusion overflowing with gratitude and delight at seeing the warm and widespread interest that was now taken in forwarding the favorite project of his life. Its piety is displayed in the fervor of devotional feeling--in the ascription of all worldly wealth and greatness to God as the giver, in tracing the general readiness in contributing to the influence of His grace, in praying for the continuance of this happy disposition among the people, and in solemnly and earnestly commending the young king and his kingdom to the care and blessing of God. <div eID="gen5629" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c28f8b894d2a16784fcc5b8eaa1b5e459696c76: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3912"/><div sID="gen5632" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3912"/><hi type="bold">20. all the congregation ... worshipped the Lord, and the king--</hi>Though the external attitude might be the same, the sentiments of which it was expressive were very different in the two cases--of divine worship in the one, of civil homage in the other. <div eID="gen5632" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd5b6947e77d37dae8ef3e8c94de3ee2b0c48e80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3913"/><div sID="gen5633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3913"/><hi type="bold">21-22. they sacrificed ... And did eat and drink--</hi>After the business of the assembly was over, the people, under the exciting influence of the occasion, still remained, and next day engaged in the performance of solemn rites, and afterwards feasted on the remainder of the sacrifices. <div eID="gen5633" type="x-p"/>
entries.2f673ac7374373f28d2f7458d40623bf38266bb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3915"/><div sID="gen5637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3915"/><hi type="bold">23. Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord--</hi>As king of Israel, he was the Lord's vicegerent. <div eID="gen5637" type="x-p"/>
entries.1da727e1d1c1f2b6840da2392ccd046039dd6691: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3916"/><div sID="gen5638" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3916"/><hi type="bold">24. submitted themselves--</hi>Hebrew, "put their hands under Solomon," according to the custom still practised in the East of putting a hand under the king's extended hand and kissing the back of it (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.15">2Ki 10:15</reference>).<div eID="gen5638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5639" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.30">1Ch 29:26-30</reference>. His Reign and Death. <div eID="gen5639" type="x-p"/>
entries.ece63bd0be3f9f9529070a02df3806af976ca70a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3917"/><div sID="gen5640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3917"/><hi type="bold">26. Thus David ... reigned--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.11">1Ki 2:11</reference>). <chapter eID="1Chr.29"/><div eID="gen5640" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5161" osisID="1Chr" type="book"/>

entries.21a57a9013cdabb0142b5b4addb2c90f787f26aa: <div eID="gen13884" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13886" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13885" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13887" type="x-p"/> David enumerates the gifts which he designed for the building of the temple; and exhorts the princes and people to make their offerings, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1-1Chr.29.5">1Chr 29:1-5</reference>. They offer willingly, and to a great amount, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6-1Chr.29.9">1Chr 29:6-9</reference>. David's thanksgiving and prayer to God on the occasion, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10-1Chr.29.19">1Chr 29:10-19</reference>. The princes and people praise God, offer sacrifices and feasts before him, make Solomon King, and do him homage, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.20-1Chr.29.24">1Chr 29:20-24</reference>. The Lord magnifies Solomon, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.25">1Chr 29:25</reference>. Concluding account of David's reign, character, and death, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.30">1Chr 29:26-30</reference>. <div eID="gen13887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13888" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13889" type="x-p"/> The palace is not for man - "The palace is not prepared for the name of a son of man, but for the name of the Word of the Lord God." - T.
entries.5d3e282d0bf29ded531e68637595171464c6fa8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13890" type="x-p"/> And marble stones - אבני שיש abney shayish, which the Vulgate translates marmor Parium, Parian marble. Paros was one of the Cyclade islands, and produced the whitest and finest marble, that of which most of the finest works of antiquity have been made. That the word shaish means marble is probable from the Chaldee, which has אבני מרמורייה abney marmoraiyah, marble stones. Josephus says that the temple was built of large blocks of white marble, beautifully polished, so as to produce a most splendid appearance. - Jos., De Bell. Jud., lib. v., c. 5, s. 2.
entries.d6aa36075c14858c3079be65062a438b6be1f71b: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen13890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13891" type="x-p"/> To consecrate his service - למלאות ידו lemalloth yado, to fill his hand; to bring an offering to the Lord.
entries.7c5e776a3d9bb27769702fbadd2b7d6653a1c55a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13892" type="x-p"/> Of gold five thousand talents - These, at five thousand and seventy-five pounds, fifteen shillings, and seven pence halfpenny each, amount to twenty-five millions, three hundred and seventy-eight thousand nine hundred and six pounds, five shillings, sterling. If, with Dr. Prideaux, we estimate the golden talent at upwards of seven thousand pounds sterling, the value of these five thousand talents will be much more considerable. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.25.39">Exo 25:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.18.24">Mat 18:24</reference>; and the calculations at the end of the notes on <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Chr 9:29</reference>. <div eID="gen13892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13893" type="x-p"/> Ten thousand drams - Probably golden darics, worth each about twenty shillings, amounting to ten thousand pounds. <div eID="gen13893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13894" type="x-p"/> Of silver ten thousand talents - These, at three hundred and fifty-three pounds, eleven shillings, and ten-pence halfpenny, each, amount to three millions five hundred and thirty-five thousand, nine hundred and thirty-seven pounds, ten shillings, sterling. <div eID="gen13894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13895" type="x-p"/> Brass eighteen thousand talents - Each six hundred and fifty-seven thousand grains, amount to one thousand and twenty-six tons, eleven hundred weight, and one quarter. <div eID="gen13895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13896" type="x-p"/> One hundred thousand talents of iron - Each six hundred and fifty-seven thousand grains, amount to five thousand seven hundred and three tons, two hundred weight, and a half.
entries.04628abc5ae038890b617b80c24361c6e1631cd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen13896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13897" type="x-p"/> Thine, O Lord, is the greatness - This verse is thus paraphrased by the Targum: "Thine, O Lord, is the magnificence; for thou hast created the world by thy great power, and by thy might hast led our fathers out of Egypt, and with great signs hast caused them to pass through the Red Sea. Thou hast appeared gloriously on Mount Sinai, with troops of angels, in giving law to thy people. Thou hast gained the victory over Amalek; over Sihon and Og, kings of Canaan. By the splendor of thy majesty thou hast caused the sun to stand still on Gibeon, and the moon in the valley of Ajalon, until thy people, the house of Israel, were avenged of their enemies. All things that are in heaven and earth are the work of thy hands, and thou rulest over and sustainest whatsoever is in the heavens and in the earth. Thine, O Lord, is the kingdom in the firmament; and thou art exalted above the heavenly angels, and over all who are constituted rulers upon earth.
entries.ef1165849fb62a89b080a770f7c107629b5dc4b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen13897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13898" type="x-p"/> Of thine own have we given thee - "For from thy presence all good comes, and of the blessings of thy hands have we given thee." - Targum.
entries.566ea9d133350461f2136863c4a95798f2b74ecc: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen13898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13899" type="x-p"/> For we are strangers - We have here neither right nor property. <div eID="gen13899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13900" type="x-p"/> And sojourners - Lodging as it were for a night, in the mansion of another. <div eID="gen13900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13901" type="x-p"/> As were all our fathers - These were, as we are supported by thy bounty, and tenants at will to thee. <div eID="gen13901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13902" type="x-p"/> Our days on the earth are as a shadow - They are continually declining, fading, and passing away. This is the place of our sojourning, and here we have no substantial, permanent residence. <div eID="gen13902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13903" type="x-p"/> There is none abiding - However we may wish to settle and remain in this state of things, it is impossible, because every earthly form is passing swiftly away, all is in a state of revolution and decay, and there is no abiding, מקוה mikveh, no expectation, that we shall be exempt from those changes and chances to which our fathers were subjected. "As the shadow of a bird flying in the air [אויר avir] of heaven, such are our days upon the earth; nor is there any hope to any son of man that he shall live for ever." - Targum.
entries.2fcdc61a5d9cb76bb5c7de8118b78e04779b48dc: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13904" type="x-p"/> Keep this for ever - All the good dispositions which myself and my people have, came from thee; continue to support and strengthen them by the same grace by which they have been inspired!
entries.5e8f5b69790fbba37982a528cc30aff79b7038c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen13904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13905" type="x-p"/> Give unto Solomon - a perfect heart - This he did, but Solomon abused his mercies.
entries.4d1c4d60627d0b1baf8d7708be1f5045781fb2c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen13905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> Worshipped the Lord, and the king - They did reverence to God as the supreme Ruler, and to the king as his deputy.
entries.71ea290ae67d011adfbb24342ea8b216785c51eb: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen13906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> With their drink-offerings - The Targum says a thousand drink-offerings, making these libations equal in number to the other offerings. <div eID="gen13907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> And sacrifices - These were peace-offerings, offered for the people, and on the flesh of which they feasted.
entries.2e9c9b345200295427cb0de1d36da49525126bb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13909" type="x-p"/> They made Solomon - king the second time - The first time of his being anointed and proclaimed king was when his brother Adonijah affected the throne; and Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah anointed and proclaimed him in a hurry, and without pomp. See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.1.39">1Kgs 1:39</reference>. Now that all is quiet, and David his father dead, (for he was probably so at the time of the second anointing), they anointed and proclaimed him afresh, with due ceremonies, sacrifices, etc. <div eID="gen13909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13910" type="x-p"/> To be the chief governor - To be the vicegerent or deputy of Jehovah; for God never gave up his right of king in Israel; those called kings were only his lieutenants: hence it is said, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23">1Chr 29:23</reference>, "that Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord as king instead of David his father."
entries.3f249ca23425ab443093dc706f9581b49743cbd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen13910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13911" type="x-p"/> Submitted themselves - נתנו יד תחת שלמה nathenu yad tachath Shelomoh. "They gave the hand under Solomon;" they swore fealty to him. We have already seen that putting the hand under the thigh (super sectionem circumcisionis) was the form of taking an oath. See the note on <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>.
entries.456694847d27eee07739344bab6374095a6411c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen13911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13912" type="x-p"/> And he died - David, at his death, had every thing that his heart could wish. <div eID="gen13912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13913" type="x-p"/> 1. A good old age, having lived as long as living could be desirable, and having in the main enjoyed good health. <div eID="gen13913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13914" type="x-p"/> 2. Full of days; having lived till he saw every thing that he lived for either accomplished or in a state of forwardness. <div eID="gen13914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13915" type="x-p"/> 3. Full of riches; witness the immense sums left for the temple. <div eID="gen13915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13916" type="x-p"/> 4. Full of honorer; having gained more renown than any crowned head ever did, either before his time or since - laurels that are fresh to the present hour.
entries.695c363f7681bfe590a39a544850dfb86f309de6: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen13916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13917" type="x-p"/> The acts of David - first and last - Those which concerned him in private life, as well as those which grew out of his regal government. All these were written by three eminent men, personally acquainted with him through the principal part of his life; these were Samuel and Gad the seers, and Nathan the prophet. These writings are all lost, except the particulars interspersed in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles, none of which are the records mentioned here.
entries.a55c1adab0b94fd095c9eeb00942a3e5c0002609: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen13917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13918" type="x-p"/> The times that went over him - The transactions of his reign, and the occurrences and vicissitudes in his own kingdom, as well as those which were over all the kingdoms of the countries, i.e., in the surrounding nations, in most of which David had a share during his forty years' reign. Relative to the character of David, see a few remarks in the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.10">1Kgs 2:10</reference> (note); and see more at the end of the Psalms. <div eID="gen13918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13919" type="x-p"/> Dr. Delaney gives a just view of his character in a few words: "To sum up all, David was a true believer, a zealous adorer of God, teacher of his law and worship, and inspirer of his praise. A glorious example, a perpetual and inexhaustible fountain of true piety. A consummate and unequalled hero; a skillful and fortunate captain; a steady patriot; a wise ruler; a faithful, generous, and magnanimous friend; and, what is yet rarer, a no less generous and magnanimous enemy. A true penitent, a divine musician, a sublime poet, and an inspired prophet. By birth, a peasant; by merit, a prince; in youth, a hero; in manhood, a monarch; and in age, a saint." The matter of Uriah and Bath-sheba is his great but only blot! There he sinned deeply; and no man ever suffered more in his body, soul, and domestic affairs, than he did in consequence. His penitence was as deep and as extraordinary as his crime; and nothing could surpass both but that eternal mercy that took away the guilt, assuaged the sorrow, and restored this most humbled transgressor to character, holiness, and happiness. Let the God of David be exalted for ever!  <chapter eID="1Chr.29"/> <div eID="gen13919" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen13325" osisID="1Chr" type="book"/>

entries.1c6a1dd55859f0b7a841f37a210d5b6f63fe633f: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1-1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:1-2</reference> <hi type="italic">Contributions of the collected princes for the building of the temple</hi>. - David then turns to the assembled princes to press upon them the furthering of the building of the temple. After referring to the youth of his son, and to the greatness of the work to be accomplished (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1">1Ch 29:1</reference>), he mentions what materials he has prepared for the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:2</reference>); then further states what he has resolved to give in addition from his private resources (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.4">1Ch 29:4</reference>); and finally, after this introduction, calls upon those present to make a voluntary collection for this great work (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">1Ch 29:5</reference>). The words, “as only one hath God chosen him,” form a parenthesis, which is to be translated as a relative sentence for “my son, whom alone God hath chosen.” ורך נער as in 1Ch 22:5. The work is great, because not for man the palace, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> is intended, i.e., shall be built, but for Jahve God. הבּירה, the citadel, the palace; a later word, generally used of the residence of the Persian king (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.2">Est 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.5">Est 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.2.3">Est 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.1.1">Neh 1:1</reference>), only in <reference osisRef="Neh.2.8">Neh 2:8</reference> of the citadel by the temple; here transferred to the temple as the glorious palace of Jahve, the God-king of Israel. With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.29.2">1Ch 29:2</reference></hi>, cf. 1Ch 22:14. וגו לזּהב הזּהב, the gold for the golden, etc., i.e., for the vessels and ornaments of gold, cf. 1Ch 28:14. וּמלּוּאים שׁהם אבני as in <reference osisRef="Exod.25.7">Exo 25:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.35.9">Exo 35:9</reference>, precious stones for the ephod and choshen. שׁהם, probably beryl. מּלּוּאים אבני, stones of filling, that is, precious stones which are put in settings. פּוּך אבני, stones of pigment, i.e., ornament, conjecturally precious stones which, from their black colour, were in appearance like פּוּך, <hi type="italic">stibium</hi>, a common eye pigment (see 2Ki 9:30). רקמה אבני, stones of variegated colour, i.e., with veins of different colours. יקרה אבן, precious stones, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.6">2Ch 3:6</reference>, for ornamenting the walls. שׁישׁ אבני, white marble stones.
entries.08595a5c4f9488b8b0c23e12038ac7b6d8fa71b6: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.3">1Ch 29:3</reference> “And moreover, because I have pleasure in the house of my God, there is to me a treasure of gold and silver; it have I appointed for the house of my God over and above all that...” הכינותי with כּל without the relative, cf. 1Ch 15:12.
entries.28e2a4848af7c41ea944d5c4c414c2de631198fb: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.4">1Ch 29:4</reference> <div eID="gen5900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> Gold 3000 talents, i.e., about 13 1/2, or, reckoning according to the royal shekel, 6 3/4 millions of pounds; 7000 talents of silver, circa 2 1/2 or 1 1/4 millions of pounds: see on 1Ch 22:14. Gold of Ophir, i.e., the finest, best gold, corresponding to the pure silver. לטוּח, to overlay the inner walls of the houses with gold and silver leaf. הבּתים as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.11">1Ch 28:11</reference>, the different buildings of the temple. The walls of the holy place and of the most holy, of the porch and of the upper chambers, were overlaid with gold (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.4-2Chr.3.6">2Ch 3:4-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.3.8-2Chr.3.9">2Ch 3:8-9</reference>), and probably only the inner walls of the side buildings.
entries.7d5dedcd3e52a3728182b3178e6661328d3a49e0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.5">1Ch 29:5</reference> לזּהב לזּהב, for every golden thing, etc., cf. 1Ch 29:2. וּלכל־מלאכה, and in general for every work to be wrought by the hands of the artificer. וּמי, who then is willing (uw expressing it as the consequence). To fill one’s hand to the Lord, means to provide oneself with something which one brings to the Lord; see on Exo 32:29. The infinitive מלּאות occurs also in <reference osisRef="Exod.31.5">Exo 31:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.9.4">Dan 9:4</reference>, and along with מלּא,   2Ch 13:9.
entries.823f00f4e2e459dc956d2416fa9525d1839129b1: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.6-1Chr.29.8">1Ch 29:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen5901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> The princes follow the example, and willingly respond to David’s call. האבות שׂרי = האבות ראשׁי,   <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.31">1Ch 24:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.1">1Ch 27:1</reference>, etc. הם מלאכת ולשׂרי, and as regards the princes of the work of the king. The למּלך וּמקנה רכוּשׁ שׂרי, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.1">1Ch 28:1</reference>, the officials enumerated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.25-1Chr.27.31">1Ch 27:25-31</reference> are meant; on ל see on 1Ch 28:21. They gave 5000 talents of gold (22 1/2 or 11 1/2 millions of pounds), and 1000 darics = 11 1/2 millions of pounds. אדרכּון, with א <hi type="italic">prosth</hi>. here and in Ezr 8:27, and דּרכּמון, Ezr 2:69; Neh 7:70., does not correspond to the Greek δραχμή, Arab. <hi type="italic">dirhem</hi>, but to the Greek δαρεικός, as the Syrian translation <hi type="italic">derîkônā'</hi>, Ezr 8:27, shows; a Persian gold coin worth about 22s. 6d. See the description of these coins, of which several specimens still exist, in Cavedoni <hi type="italic">bibl. Numismatik, übers</hi>. von A. Werlhof, S. 84ff.; J. Brandis, <hi type="italic">das Münz-Mass und Gewishtssystem in Vorderasien</hi> (1866), S. 244; and my <hi type="italic">bibl. Archäol</hi>. §127, 3. “Our historian uses the words used in his time to designate the current gold coins, without intending to assume that there were darics in use in the time of David, to state in a way intelligible to his readers the amount of the sum contributed by the princes” (Bertheau). This perfectly correct remark does not, however, explain why the author of the Chronicle has stated the contribution in gold and that in silver in different values, in talents and in darics, since the second cannot be an explanation of the first, the two sums being different. Probably the sum in darics is the amount which they contributed in gold pieces received as coins; the talents, on the other hand, probably represent the weight of the vessels and other articles of gold which they brought as offerings for the building. The amount contributed in silver is not large when compared with that in gold: 10,000 talents = £3,500,000, or one half that amount. The contribution in copper also, 18,000 talents, is not very large. Besides these, those who had stones, i.e., precious stones, also brought them. אתּו הנּמצא, that was found with him, for: that which he (each one) had of stones they gave. The sing. אתּו is to be taken distributively, and is consequently carried on in the plural, נתנוּ; cf. Ew. §319, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. אבנים is <hi type="italic">accus</hi>. of subordination. יד על נתן, to give over for administration (Ew. §282, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). יחיאל, the Levite family of this name which had the oversight of the treasures of the house of God (1Ch 26:21.).
entries.e3a78ad49a43549e81652dac0e3d72042288c718: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.9">1Ch 29:9</reference> <div eID="gen5902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> The people and the king rejoiced over this willingness to give. שׁלם בּלב, as in 1Ch 28:9.
entries.52429ba3be5c30f3dcf05c767f691a875b9bb949: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10-1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:10-11</reference> <hi type="italic">David’s thanksgiving prayer</hi>. - David gives fitting expression to his joy on the success of the deepest wish of his heart, in a prayer with which he closes the last parliament of his reign. Since according to the divine decree, not he, the man of war, but his son, the peace-king Solomon, was to build a temple to the Lord, David had taken it upon himself to prepare as far as possible for the carrying out of the work. He had also found the princes and chiefs of the people willing to further it, and to assist his son Solomon in it. In this the pious and grey-haired servant of the Lord saw a special proof of the divine favour, for which he must thank God the Lord before the whole congregation. He praises Jahve, “the God of Israel our father,” <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10">1Ch 29:10</reference>, or, as it is in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.18">1Ch 29:18</reference>, “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, our fathers.” Jahve had clearly revealed himself to David and his people as the God of Israel and of the patriarchs, by fulfilling in so glorious a manner to the people of Israel, by David, the promises made to the patriarchs. God the Lord had not only by David made His people great and powerful, and secured to them the peaceful possession of the good land, by humbling all their enemies round about, but He had also awakened in the heart of the people such love to and trust in their God, that the assembled dignitaries of the kingdom showed themselves perfectly willing to assist in furthering the building of the house of God. In this God had revealed His greatness, power, glory, etc., as David (in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.11">1Ch 29:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.12">1Ch 29:12</reference>) acknowledges with praise: “Thine, Jahve, is the greatness,” etc. הנּצח, according to the Aramaic usage, gloria, splendour, honour. כל כּי, yea all, still dependent on לך at the commencement of the sentence, so that we do not need to supply לך after כּי. “Thine is the dominion, and the raising of oneself to be head over all.” In His ממלכה God reveals His greatness, might, glory, etc. ממנשּׂא is not a participle requiring אתּה, “thou art,” to be supplied (Berth.), but an appellative, an Aramaic infinitive, - the raising oneself (Ew. §160, <hi type="italic">e</hi>).
entries.946c554028a2a8cd78599bb4162177e5b3195295: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.12">1Ch 29:12</reference> “From Thee came the riches and the glory ..., and in Thy hand is it (it lies) to make all things great and strong.”
entries.420738ec62ee8f747fe691854ed72a6325a05a06: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.13">1Ch 29:13</reference> <div eID="gen5903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5904" type="x-p"/> For this we must thank God, and sing praise to His holy name. By the partic. מודים, from הודה, confess, praise, the praising of God is characterized as an enduring praise, always rising anew.
entries.d950cf754644f4a6201e4eeec5d2ad28d086b129: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">1Ch 29:14</reference> <div eID="gen5904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5905" type="x-p"/> For man of himself can give nothing: “What am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to show ourselves so liberal?” כּוח עצר כּוח, to hold strength together; both to have power to do anything (here and <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.5">2Ch 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.9">2Ch 22:9</reference>), and also to retain strength (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">2Ch 13:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.10.8">Dan 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.10.16">Dan 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.6">Dan 11:6</reference>), only found in Daniel and in the Chronicle. התנדּב, to show oneself willing, especially in giving. כּזאת refers to the contribution to the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.3-1Chr.29.8">1Ch 29:3-8</reference>). From Thy hand, i.e., that which is received from Thee, have we given.
entries.2f3466382b381f4f461328b0dcd6d509a6b78b2b: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.15">1Ch 29:15</reference> <div eID="gen5905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5906" type="x-p"/> For we are strangers (as <reference osisRef="Ps.39.13">Psa 39:13</reference>), i.e., in this connection we have no property, no enduring possession, since God had only given them the usufruct of the land; and as of the land, so also of all the property of man, it is only a gift committed to us by God in usufruct. The truth that our life is a pilgrimage (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.12-Heb.11.14">Heb 11:12-14</reference>), is presented to us by the brevity of life. As a shadow, so swiftly passing away, are our days upon the earth (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.8.9">Job 8:9</reference>; Psa 90:9., <reference osisRef="Ps.102.12">Psa 102:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.4">Psa 144:4</reference>). מקוה ואין, and there is no trust, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> in the continuance of life (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.8">Jer 14:8</reference>).
entries.548a41ee836a6ccbb761bb11154a3c4f740fa080: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.16">1Ch 29:16</reference> <div eID="gen5906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5907" type="x-p"/> All the riches which we have prepared for the building of the temple come from the hand of God. The Keth. הוּא is neuter, the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> הוּא corresponds to ההמון.
entries.9dd5c5be2df498dfbd586c15b4f1029921bf2f16: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.17">1Ch 29:17</reference> <div eID="gen5907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5908" type="x-p"/> Before God, who searches the heart and loves uprightness, David can declare that he has willingly given in uprightness of heart, and that the people also have, to his joy, shown equal willingness. כּל־אלּה, all the treasures enumerated (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.3-1Chr.29.8">1Ch 29:3-8</reference>). The plural הנּמצאוּ refers to עמּך, and the demonstrative ה stands for אשׁר as in 1Ch 26:28.
entries.e2fd68cfec75564fe412e6f86ab6c5f77e953189: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.18">1Ch 29:18</reference> <div eID="gen5908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5909" type="x-p"/> He prays that God may enable the people ever to retain this frame of heart. זאת is more closely defined by מח ליצר, viz., the frame of the thoughts of the heart of Thy people. “And direct their heart (the people’s heart) to Thee,” cf. 1Sa 7:3.
entries.de710490af59fe4a843fa16e24b71187bcc9cd7e: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.19">1Ch 29:19</reference> <div eID="gen5909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5910" type="x-p"/> And to Solomon may God give a whole (undivided) heart, that he may keep all the divine commands and do them, and build the temple. שׁלם לב as in 1Ch 29:9. הכּל לעשׂות, that he may do all, <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> that the commands, testimonies, and statutes require. For הבּירה, see 1Ch 29:1.
entries.117bf7ffa7470207975c39e2e55c6f9cc5683109: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.20">1Ch 29:20</reference> <hi type="italic">Close of the public assembly</hi>. - 1Ch 29:20. At the conclusion of the prayer, David calls upon the whole assembly to praise God; which they do, bowing before God and the king, and worshipping. וישׁתּחווּ יקּדוּ, connected as in <reference osisRef="Exod.4.31">Exo 4:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.43.28">Gen 43:28</reference>, etc.
entries.1ab09e6cb789529b2819a8343400dacffdc3d0f2: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.21">1Ch 29:21</reference> <div eID="gen5910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5911" type="x-p"/> To seal their confession, thus made in word and deed, the assembled dignitaries prepared a great sacrificial feast to the Lord on the following day. They sacrificed to the Lord sacrifices, viz., 1000 bullocks, 1000 rams, and 1000 lambs as burnt-offering, with drink-offerings to correspond, and sacrifices, i.e., thank-offerings (שׁלמים), in multitude for all Israel, i.e., so that all those present could take part in the sacrificial meal prepared from these sacrifices. While זבהים in the first clause is the general designation of the bloody offerings as distinguished from the meat-offerings, in the last clause it is restricted by the contrast with עלות and the שׁלמים, from which joyous sacrificial meals were prepared.
entries.5ae68e0b61ddfb306e3d5c2762196b010ac748b0: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.22">1Ch 29:22</reference> <div eID="gen5911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5912" type="x-p"/> On this day they made Solomon king a second time, anointing him king to the Lord, and Zadok to be priest, i.e., high priest. The שׁנית refers back to <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.1">1Ch 23:1</reference>, and the first anointing of Solomon narrated in 1Ki 1:32. ליהיה, not: before Jahve, which ל cannot signify, but: “to Jahve,” in accordance with His will expressed in His choice of Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.4">1Ch 28:4</reference>). The ל before צדוק is <hi type="italic">nota accus</hi>., as in לשׁלמה. From the last words we learn that Zadok received the high-priesthood with the consent of the estates of the kingdom.
entries.6b19abc53018cacd28ee5023894f59a317eeafd4: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23-1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:23-24</reference> <hi type="italic">Solomon’s accession and David’s death</hi>, with a statement as to the length of his reign and the sources of the history. - <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.23">1Ch 29:23</reference>-25. The remarks on Solomon’s accession and reign contained in these verses are necessary to the complete conclusion of a history of David’s reign, for they show how David’s wishes for his son Solomon, whom Jahve chose to be his successor, were fulfilled. On יהוה על־כּסּא see the commentary on 1Ch 28:5. ויּצלח, he was prosperous, corresponds to the hope expressed by David (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">1Ch 22:13</reference>), which was also fulfilled by the submission of all princes and heroes, and also of all the king’s sons, to King Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.24">1Ch 29:24</reference>). There can hardly, however, be in these last words a reference to the frustrating of Adonijah’s attempted usurpation of the throne (cf. 1Ki 1:15.). תּחת יד נתן = to submit. But this meaning is not derived (Rashi) from the custom of taking oaths of fidelity by clasping of hands, for this custom cannot be certainly proved to have existed among the Israelites; still less can it have arisen from the ancient custom mentioned in <reference osisRef="Gen.24.2">Gen 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.9">Gen 24:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.47.29">Gen 47:29</reference>, of laying the hand under the thigh of the person to whom one swore in making promises with oath. The hand, as the instrument of all activity, is here simply a symbol of power.
entries.47698fcd82bc1d4a86ea0a4d3acb924f0e981cbe: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.25">1Ch 29:25</reference> <div eID="gen5912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5913" type="x-p"/> Jahve made Solomon very great, by giving him the glory of the kingdom, as no king before him had had it. כּל is to be taken along with לא, <hi type="italic">nullus</hi>, and does not presuppose a number of kings before Solomon; it involves only more than one. Before him, Saul, Ishbosheth, and David had been kings, and the kingship of the latter had been covered with glory.
entries.f7e56b1b4134197899ee92fe44adcb88c93bfaf7: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.26-1Chr.29.27">1Ch 29:26-27</reference> כּל־ישׂראל על (as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1">1Ch 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.38">1Ch 12:38</reference>), referring to the fact that David had been for a time king only over Judah, but had been recognised at a later time by all the tribes of Israel as king. The length of his reign as in 1Ki 2:11. In Hebron seven years; according to <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.5">2Sa 5:5</reference>, more exactly seven years and six months.
entries.2357b69315c27fdcd3c0876485d4be4447d071f7: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.28">1Ch 29:28</reference> <div eID="gen5913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5914" type="x-p"/> On וכבוד עשׁר cf. 1Ki 3:13; 2Ch 17:5.
entries.e2e84dbfe61a55aacb1d26efef2d5684a1cb50b8: <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29-1Chr.29.30">1Ch 29:29-30</reference> <div eID="gen5914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5915" type="x-p"/> On the authorities cited see the Introduction. וגו כּל־מלכוּתו עם goes with כּתוּבים הנּם: the acts of David ... are written ... together with his whole reign and his power, and the times which went over him. העתּים, the times, with their joys and sorrows, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">Psa 31:16</reference>; Job 24:1. The kingdoms of the lands (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2Ch 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.10">2Ch 17:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.29">2Ch 20:29</reference>) are the kingdoms with which the Israelites under David came into contact-Philistia, Edom, Moab, Ammon, Aram.  <chapter eID="1Chr.29"/> <div eID="gen5915" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen5516" osisID="1Chr" type="book"/>
